question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13, what general duty does a Georgia landlord owe regarding the physical condition of the rental premises during the tenancy?
choice_a: Georgia law places the entire repair burden on the tenant with no landlord repair duty of any kind
choice_b: The landlord's repair duty applies only during the first 30 days of the lease term
choice_c: The landlord must keep the premises in repair, and is liable for substantial improvements placed on the premises with the landlord's consent
choice_d: The landlord's repair duty applies only to commercial leases, never residential leases
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13 states that the landlord must keep the premises in repair, and is liable for substantial improvements placed on the premises with the landlord's consent -- a general statutory repair obligation running for the duration of the tenancy.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2, may the landlord's repair duty under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13 be waived by agreement between landlord and tenant?
choice_a: Yes -- landlords and tenants may freely waive any statutory duty by including a lease clause to that effect
choice_b: Yes, but only if the tenant is a commercial entity rather than an individual
choice_c: The repair duty may be waived only with GREC's prior written approval
choice_d: No -- O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2 specifically prohibits landlords and tenants from waiving the rights set out in the repair-and-improvements provisions
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2 specifically bars landlords and tenants from contracting away the rights established in the repair-and-improvements provisions (including O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13) -- a lease clause purporting to waive the landlord's repair duty would not be enforceable.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2, up to what lease term may a Georgia landlord-tenant relationship be created by a purely oral (parol) agreement, without violating the statute of frauds?
choice_a: Any term not exceeding one year
choice_b: Any term at all, with no limitation on oral leases
choice_c: No oral lease is ever valid in Georgia regardless of term length
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2 provides that a landlord-tenant relationship for any time not exceeding one year may be created by parol (oral) agreement -- a specific statute-of-frauds carve-out for shorter-term leases, distinct from the general writing requirement for land-sale contracts and longer leases.

question: Under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2, if a residential lease contains a clause requiring only the tenant (and not the landlord) to pay the other party's attorney's fees in litigation over the lease, is that clause enforceable?
choice_a: Yes -- landlords may always include a one-way attorney's-fee clause favoring themselves with no restriction
choice_b: No -- O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2 voids a one-way attorney's-fee-shifting provision unless it is reciprocal, obligating both parties equally
choice_c: Yes, provided the clause is initialed separately by the tenant
choice_d: The enforceability of attorney's-fee clauses is entirely unaddressed by Georgia landlord-tenant law
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 44-7-2 voids a lease provision requiring the tenant to pay the landlord's attorney's fees unless the obligation is made reciprocal -- a one-sided fee-shifting clause favoring only the landlord is unenforceable.

question: As a matter of general property-management leasing practice (not itself a specific Georgia statutory citation), what is the practical distinction between a tenant 'assigning' a lease and 'subletting' the premises?
choice_a: The two terms are legally identical in every jurisdiction and every context
choice_b: An assignment always requires a brand-new written lease document, while a subletting never requires any writing
choice_c: An assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining leasehold interest to a new party, who then deals directly with the landlord, while a subletting creates a new, separate landlord-tenant relationship between the original tenant and a subtenant, with the original tenant remaining primarily liable to the landlord
choice_d: Subletting automatically releases the original tenant from all further liability to the landlord, while an assignment never does
explanation: As a matter of general leasing doctrine, an assignment transfers the entire remaining leasehold interest to the assignee, who then stands in direct privity with the landlord, whereas a sublet creates a separate landlord-subtenant-like relationship in which the original tenant typically remains primarily liable to the landlord for lease compliance.
source_note: hedge: standard national landlord-tenant leasing doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

question: As a matter of general property-management practice, what is the purpose of a documented move-in/move-out condition report (inspection checklist) for a managed rental unit?
choice_a: It has no practical value and is purely a formality with no bearing on deposit disputes
choice_b: It is required solely to satisfy fair housing advertising rules
choice_c: It replaces the landlord's obligation to provide any itemized statement of deductions under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34
choice_d: It creates an objective, dated record of the unit's condition at the start and end of the tenancy, helping to substantiate (or refute) proposed security deposit deductions and reducing the risk of disputes over pre-existing versus tenant-caused damage
explanation: A documented condition report at move-in and move-out creates an objective record that helps substantiate legitimate deposit deductions (or protect the tenant from improper ones), reducing disputes over whether damage was pre-existing or tenant-caused -- though it does not itself substitute for the landlord's separate statutory itemization obligation under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-34.
source_note: hedge: standard national property-management risk-management practice

question: A residential lease term expires, but the tenant remains in possession and continues paying rent, which the landlord accepts, without either party signing a new lease. As a matter of general landlord-tenant doctrine, what tenancy typically results?
choice_a: A holdover tenancy generally results, commonly treated as a periodic (e.g., month-to-month) tenancy on the prior lease's material terms, formed by the landlord's acceptance of continued rent after the original lease term expired
choice_b: The lease automatically terminates immediately with no further tenancy of any kind, regardless of continued rent acceptance
choice_c: The tenant automatically acquires fee simple ownership of the property after 30 days of holdover
choice_d: A holdover tenant can never be lawfully removed under any circumstances once the original lease expires
explanation: When a tenant remains in possession after lease expiration and the landlord accepts continued rent, this generally creates a holdover tenancy -- commonly treated as a periodic tenancy (such as month-to-month) continuing on the prior lease's material terms, as a matter of general landlord-tenant doctrine.
source_note: hedge: standard national landlord-tenant holdover-tenancy doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific
